title: Immune memory
log: 2026-10-27T00:53:12Z write: the API refused it in the chapter request, so it is written on its own next

draft.title: Immune memory
card: During a first infection, some B cells and T cells that matched the pathogen's antigen become memory cells. These cells stay in the body for years, sometimes for life.
If the same pathogen enters again, memory cells recognise its antigen straight away. They divide quickly and form many more cells that act against it.
The second response (secondary response) is faster and stronger than the first. More antibodies are made in less time, so the pathogen is often cleared before the person feels ill.
Memory cells are specific. They match only the antigen that caused the first infection, so a different pathogen starts a new, slower first response.
draft.remember: Memory cells let the body respond faster and harder to a pathogen it has met before.

a.q: Why is the immune response to a second exposure to the same pathogen faster than the first?
opts: Memory cells already recognise its antigen
Antibodies from the first infection stay at full level
The innate response learns to target that pathogen
The skin blocks the pathogen before it can enter
a.why: Memory cells formed in the first infection recognise the antigen at once and divide quickly. The first response is slower because it starts with few cells that match the antigen. Saying the innate response learns is wrong, as memory belongs to B cells and T cells, which are specific.
a.clue: Think about which cells are left behind after the first infection.

b.q: Priya had chickenpox as a child and did not get it again when exposed years later. She then catches a cold caused by a virus she has never met. Which statement is correct?
opts: The cold virus starts a slower first response
Her memory cells make the cold response faster
Her chickenpox memory cells will also stop the cold virus
She has no immune response to the cold virus
b.why: Memory cells match only the antigen that caused the first infection. The cold virus has different antigens, so it triggers a new first response, which is slower. The tempting idea that memory cells help against any virus is wrong because they are specific.
b.clue: Do chickenpox memory cells match the antigens of a different virus?

a.best: Memory cells already recognise its antigen

b.best: The cold virus starts a slower first response
